subtopic: The Modulus and the Conjugate of a Complex Number
title: Triangle inequality & parallelogram identity

board_content.text: The modulus does NOT distribute over a sum — only $\le$ holds.
Equality holds only when the two point the same way (one a non-negative real multiple of the other).

board_content.text: The parallelogram identity: the two diagonals and the two sides are locked together.

segments_english.text: Modulus is multiplicative, and that was clean. But under addition it behaves differently, and this is where mistakes cluster.
The triangle inequality says: the modulus of z one plus z two is less than or equal to the modulus of z one plus the modulus of z two.
Read the warning carefully. The modulus does not distribute over a sum. It is only ever less than or equal, never automatically equal.
Equality is special: it holds only when the two numbers point in the same direction, that is, when one is a non-negative real multiple of the other.
The name comes straight from geometry. Draw z one, then z two starting where z one ended; the straight closing side, z one plus z two, can never be longer than going around the two other sides.
There's a companion lower bound too: the size of the difference of the moduli is at most the modulus of the difference.
And a beautiful equality, the parallelogram identity: the modulus of the sum squared plus the modulus of the difference squared equals two times the sum of the individual moduli squared.
Geometrically that says the two diagonals of a parallelogram and its two sides are rigidly locked together — a fact you can quote directly in proofs.

segments_hinglish.text: Modulus multiplicative tha, aur wo clean tha. Par addition ke under ye alag behave karta hai, aur yahin mistakes cluster hoti hain.
Triangle inequality kehti hai: z one plus z two ka modulus less than or equal to hai z one ke modulus plus z two ke modulus.
Warning dhyaan se padho. Modulus sum par distribute nahi karta. Ye hamesha sirf less than or equal hai, kabhi automatically equal nahi.
Equality special hai: ye tabhi hoti hai jab dono numbers same direction mein point karein, yaani jab ek doosre ka non-negative real multiple ho.
Naam geometry se seedha aata hai. z one banao, phir z two wahan se jahan z one khatam hua; seedhi closing side, z one plus z two, kabhi do doosri sides ke around jaane se lambi nahi ho sakti.
Ek companion lower bound bhi hai: moduli ke difference ka size at most difference ke modulus jitna hai.
Aur ek khoobsurat equality, parallelogram identity: sum ke modulus squared plus difference ke modulus squared barabar two times individual moduli squared ka sum.
Geometrically ye kehti hai ki parallelogram ke do diagonals aur uski do sides rigidly locked hain — ek fact jo aap proofs mein seedhe quote kar sakte ho.
